planting.note: Germinate whole nuts on their sides in a nursery bed or large pot, then move the seedling to its permanent coastal or lowland tropical spot once several leaves have formed.

directions: King Coconut is a naturally occurring botanical variety of coconut long cultivated in Sri Lanka's wet and intermediate coastal lowlands, distinguished by its bright orange husk and shorter, less massive trunk than tall plantation coconut types. It is grown almost exclusively for its sweet, electrolyte-rich drinking water rather than copra or coconut oil, with roadside vendors across Sri Lanka selling the chilled nuts whole. Because it is self-pollinating and fairly uniform from seed, growers can raise productive palms from selected nuts without grafting, though first harvests take several years. Plant in deep, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun with reliable moisture, and expect large bunches of orange-husked nuts once the palm matures.
sources: Sri Lanka National Coconut Research Institute (NCRI)
Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Coconut Genetic Resources

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; TRI 2025 is best suited to USDA zones 9-11.

directions: Released by Sri Lanka's Tea Research Institute from an open-pollinated Assam-type parent, TRI 2025 is one of the most widely planted clonal cultivars in the island's lower-elevation tea districts, valued for long, thick leaves that translate into one of the heaviest shoot yields among Ceylon clones. Its productivity rises further at higher elevations, making it a flexible choice across a range of growing sites. Grow it with the same acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture required by other tea camellias, and pluck the top two leaves and a bud on a frequent rotation to keep the bush in steady production. It has also served as a parent in later Sri Lankan tea breeding programs aimed at region-specific clones.
sources: Tea Research Institute of Sri Lanka

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; TRI 777 performs best in cool, high-elevation tropical sites equivalent to USDA zones 9-11.

directions: Released in 1958 by Sri Lanka's Tea Research Institute from Indo-Chinese seedling stock (Shan Cho Long No. 777), TRI 777 was selected for the up-country growing region and has long been recognized as a benchmark high-quality clone, consistently showing some of the richest polyphenol and catechin levels measured among Ceylon cultivars. That chemistry translates into made tea prized for depth of flavor, and the clone has since been used as a breeding parent for newer Sri Lankan tea cultivars. Grow it in cool, acidic, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture at higher elevation for the best cup quality, plucking the top two leaves and a bud on a regular cycle. It remains a useful quality reference clone against which newer introductions are measured.
sources: Tea Research Institute of Sri Lanka

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun once risk of chilly nights has passed.

directions: Also called the Jaffna mango, Karutha Colomban is one of Sri Lanka's most widely grown and sought-after traditional mango selections, ripening to a large, oval, yellow-skinned fruit with fiberless, deep yellow flesh and a sweet, mildly tangy Indochinese-type flavor. The tree grows into a dense, upright, vigorous canopy and fruits heavily during Sri Lanka's yala season from roughly May through August, tolerating the wet tropical conditions of the island better than many other mango selections. Graft onto seedling rootstock for earlier, more predictable bearing, and plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with protection from strong wind while young. Established trees need only supplemental water during extended dry spells once their deep root systems are in place.
sources: ResearchGate: Morphometric analysis of mango varieties in Sri Lanka

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun once risk of chilly nights has passed.

directions: Brought to Sri Lanka from Mauritius in the early twentieth century under the colonial Department of Agriculture, Willard became one of the island's most widely planted commercial mango selections, especially through the drier North Central and Northwestern growing areas. Fruit is large and oval, ripening bright yellow with a red-blushed stem end and mild, juicy flesh, and the tree is noted for precocious flowering and vigorous growth that adapts to a range of well-drained soil types. Thin heavy fruit clusters down to four or five fruits per panicle to improve fruit size, and allow roughly ninety days from full bloom to harvest before picking for ripening off the tree. Give young trees full sun and deep, well-drained soil, tapering supplemental water once they are established.
sources: ResearchGate: The Mango in the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka
Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture Food Crops Research and Development Centre
